opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most important thing about our safety framework is that it isn't any single metric or test. It's a layered approach, and no one layer is sufficient on its own.

There are a few main pieces. First, simulation at scale. We replay and perturb huge numbers of real driving scenarios, and we also synthesize challenging ones, so we can see how a new release behaves across a much wider distribution than we'd ever encounter on the road in a reasonable time. A big part of my team's work is making those simulations realistic. That means the other agents have to react plausibly to what our car does, rather than just following logged trajectories. Otherwise you can draw the wrong conclusions about safety.

Second, structured testing. We run closed-course tests for rare or dangerous situations that you simply can't wait to observe naturally, and we have scenario-based evaluations targeting specific capabilities and known failure modes.

Third, real-world driving and monitoring. Ultimately you have to validate against reality, so we look at on-road performance and compare it to meaningful baselines. Increasingly that means comparing against human drivers in the same areas, on metrics like injury-causing crashes and airbag deployments. Now that we've accumulated many millions of rider-only miles, those comparisons are becoming statistically meaningful, and that's been really encouraging.

Underlying all of this is a set of acceptance criteria. We think about absence of unreasonable risk, both at the aggregate level and at the level of individual behaviors. It's not enough to be safer than humans on average. You also want to make sure you're not introducing new kinds of failures that humans wouldn't make, and that the system behaves in ways other road users can understand and anticipate.

The last thing I'd stress is that it's a continuous process. Every release goes through this gauntlet, and what we learn from deployment feeds back into new scenarios, new evaluations, and better models. As the system scales to new cities and conditions, the framework has to scale with it. That's one of the most interesting research challenges in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes a continuous feedback loop and says every release goes through validation, but it does not state that Waymo has demonstrated iterative improvement while continuing to pass the release process.

r002.rationale: It discusses comparison with human drivers, but does not distinguish validating that the system avoids getting stuck from validating that it is safer than a human.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. So when I think about what makes Waymo's safety framework important, I'd start with the fact that it isn't a single number or a single test. It's a layered approach, and that's deliberate, because driving is such an open-ended problem that no one methodology captures it on its own.

The first layer is what we call hardware and system safety, the more traditional engineering discipline. Redundant compute, redundant braking and steering, fault detection, the kind of thing you'd expect from aerospace or automotive functional safety. That's the foundation, but it's not where the hard questions live.

The second layer is behavioral safety, which is really about the driving itself. Does the system make good decisions in traffic, does it handle the situations it's actually going to encounter? Here we lean very heavily on simulation. We've driven tens of millions of real miles, but on top of that we run billions of miles in simulation, and the key thing is that simulation lets us do more than replay the past. We can take a scenario we encountered once, and perturb it, make the pedestrian step out a half second earlier, make the other car more aggressive, and generate thousands of variants. That's how you probe the long tail, because the rare, dangerous events are by definition rare in real data.

And then there's the piece I think is most interesting from a methodology standpoint, which is how you actually decide a release is ready. We use a combination of scenario-based testing, where we define collections of situations the system has to handle, and statistical evaluation against a benchmark. One thing we've done is model how a careful, attentive human driver would behave in the same situations, so we can ask not just "did we avoid the crash" but "would a good human have avoided it, and did we do at least as well?" That gives you a meaningful reference point rather than an arbitrary threshold.

What ties it all together is that it's a closed loop. Every mile driven on the road feeds back into the scenario libraries and the simulations, so each release is evaluated against a richer set of situations than the last. And I think that's the real lesson, that safety validation for a learned system isn't a gate you pass once, it's a continuous process that has to grow with the system and with the environments you deploy into.

astra-6.text:
I think the important thing is that safety validation has to be systematic and layered. You can’t reduce it to one metric, like how many miles you’ve driven or how often someone intervenes. You need to understand the situations the system will encounter, what can go wrong, and what evidence you have that it will respond safely.

For a release, that means looking both at the individual capabilities—perception, prediction, planning—and at how they work together. Simulation lets you test a broad range of scenarios, including rare and difficult situations. Controlled testing and experience on public roads provide complementary evidence. None of those is sufficient by itself.

And the question isn’t simply, “Did the new version get better on average?” You also need to ask whether it introduced a regression in a particular situation. Having a structured framework for making that decision, with clear criteria and a rigorous review of the evidence, is really important.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing is that safety validation has to be systematic and grounded in evidence. You need a framework that connects the capabilities of the system to the risks it will encounter in the environment where you intend to deploy it.

For a release, you want to understand both whether you’ve improved the system and whether you’ve introduced regressions. That requires multiple complementary ways of evaluating it. Simulation lets you test a broad range of situations, including rare and challenging ones. Testing on a closed course and driving on public roads provide additional evidence. None of those, by itself, gives you the whole picture.

And it’s not just about an aggregate number. You need to look at particular behaviors and scenarios, understand the failures, and have a disciplined process for deciding whether the evidence supports deployment. That process also needs to continue after a release, as you learn from operating the system.
